newsitem.title: UK: Stg consolidating below 3.00 marks after plunge.
newsitem.headline: Stg consolidating below 3.00 marks after plunge.

text.p: The pound hovered below 3.00 marks and around $1.63 in European morning trading as dealers pondered the next move after Monday's slide.

The scale of the sell-off on Monday meant the pound was now likely to consolidate, traders said. Sterling's 4.5-pfennig and three-cent plunge on Monday looked more like a correction than the first leg of a big pound sell-off, analysts said.
"Sterling had a fantastic rally, and if you put that into context, yesterday's fall was not quite as dramatic as it looked at first sight," said Teis Knuthsen, economist at First Chicago in London.
At 0915 GMT, sterling was at 2.9935/45 marks, above its overnight low at 2.9885 but down from 3.0130/40 late on Monday.
Against the dollar sterling was at $1.6309/16, off the overnight low at $1.6270 but down from $1.6321/26 late Monday.
The Bank of England trade-weighted index was at 104.0, down from 104.6 at the previous close.

The sell-off on Monday was partly prompted by talk the Bank of England monetary policy committee might hold off another interest rate rise when it meets next week as calls from UK exporters about the harmful strength of sterling were getting more vociferous.
But traders also pointed to a relatively thin market, which tended to exaggerate market movements.
Sterling/mark has now fallen about 2.5 percent since the European opening on Monday. But even at current levels it is still about 3 percent higher against the mark than at the start of July.
Paul Meggyesi, senior currency analyst at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell, said sterling may dip a little more in the short-term, especially if the mark benefits further from short-covering.
"But the time may not yet be ripe for a full-blown trend reversal," he said.
Predictions of a recession in UK manufacturing due to the strength of the pound were alarmist and ignored the compensating effect of rising domestic demand on growth, he said.
Consumer credit data for July released on Tuesday showed another sharp rise. Consumer credit rose 1.275 billion sterling, against a one billion increase expected by economists.
Analysts said that one of the engines of sterling's rally - the perception that Europe's single currency will be weak - was running out of steam.
"The soft euro argument has run its course, which is also reflected in the current stability of the mark's crosses," said Knuthsen at First Chicago.
